title: What Happens When You Type a URL
summary: You'll be able to walk through everything from pressing Enter to pixels on screen — URL parsing, DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, the server side and browser rendering — with realistic timings for each step.

questions.prompt: List, in order, the main **network** steps a browser takes before it receives the first byte of HTML from `https://example.com` on a cold start (nothing cached, no open connections).
keyPoints: DNS resolution of example.com to an IP address (browser/OS cache, then recursive resolver)
TCP three-way handshake to port 443 (1 RTT)
TLS handshake including certificate validation (1 RTT for TLS 1.3, 2 for TLS 1.2)
HTTP GET request sent; response arrives after 1 RTT plus server processing time
Correct order: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP (with HTTP/3, QUIC combines transport and TLS setup)

questions.prompt:
Estimate the time to first byte (TTFB) of the HTML for a user whose RTT to your server is **120 ms**. Cold start: DNS takes **60 ms**, TCP + **TLS 1.3**, server processing **40 ms**.

Then estimate it again for the *second* page they open on your site a minute later, assuming the connection was kept alive.
questions.hint: Add up: DNS + TCP RTT + TLS RTT + request RTT + server time. What can be skipped the second time?
keyPoints: Cold: 60 (DNS) + 120 (TCP) + 120 (TLS 1.3) + 120 (request RTT) + 40 (server) = 460 ms
Second page: DNS cached and connection reused, so only 120 + 40 = 160 ms
Most of the cold time is round trips, not server work
Mentions improvements: CDN edge to shrink RTT, HTTP/3 to merge handshakes, preconnect
questions.answer: Cold: `60 + 120 + 120 + 120 + 40 = 460 ms`. Second page (DNS cached, connection reused): `120 + 40 = 160 ms`. Round trips dominate; shrinking RTT (CDN/edge) or the number of round trips (connection reuse, HTTP/3) matters more than shaving server time.

questions.prompt: The HTML has arrived. Describe what the browser does to turn it into pixels on the screen. What does **render-blocking** mean, and why is a `<script src="app.js">` in the `<head>` a problem?
keyPoints: Parses HTML incrementally into the DOM tree and discovers sub-resources (CSS, JS, images), which trigger more requests
Parses CSS into the CSSOM; CSS is render-blocking (no paint until styles are ready)
A classic script in the head is parser-blocking: HTML parsing pauses while it downloads and executes
Then layout (sizes/positions), paint and compositing produce pixels
Fix: use `defer`/`async` or place scripts at the end, inline critical CSS, lazy-load images

questions.prompt: Users in Australia complain your site takes over 3 seconds to load, while US users see under 1 second. Your servers are only in `us-east`. The HTML is personalized; CSS, JS and images are static. What's causing the gap, and what would you change? Be specific about which steps each change speeds up.
questions.hint: What's the RTT from Australia to the US east coast, and how many round trips does a cold page load need?
keyPoints: RTT from Australia to us-east is roughly 200+ ms, and a cold load needs many sequential round trips (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTML, then sub-resources), so distance dominates
Put static assets on a CDN with long Cache-Control on hashed filenames, so they're served from an Australian edge
Terminate TCP/TLS at the CDN edge (short RTT handshakes), with the edge reusing warm connections to the origin for the dynamic HTML
Cut round trips: HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, preconnect/dns-prefetch, fewer origins, fewer render-blocking resources
If still too slow, deploy the app (and read replicas/caches) in an Asia-Pacific region with geo/latency-based DNS

questions.prompt:
Write a small JavaScript function `describeUrl(str)` that returns an object with the **scheme**, **host**, **port** (filling in the default 80 or 443 when not given), **path**, **query parameters** as a plain object, and a boolean `fragmentSentToServer`. Use the built-in `URL` class.

Example: `describeUrl("https://shop.example.com/cart?item=42&qty=2#reviews")`.
questions.hint: `new URL(str)` gives `protocol`, `hostname`, `port`, `pathname`, `searchParams`, `hash`. An empty `port` means the default for the scheme.
keyPoints: Uses `new URL(str)` and reads protocol (strip the trailing ':'), hostname, pathname
Fills in the default port when `url.port` is empty: 443 for https, 80 for http
Converts `searchParams` to a plain object, e.g. `Object.fromEntries(url.searchParams)`
`fragmentSentToServer` is always false: the fragment never leaves the browser
Example output: { scheme: 'https', host: 'shop.example.com', port: 443, path: '/cart', query: { item: '42', qty: '2' }, fragmentSentToServer: false }

questions.prompt: Give the full answer to **"What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?"** in about two minutes, then pick the server-side part and go one level deeper: what happens between the request reaching your infrastructure and the response leaving it, for a typical production web app?
questions.hint: Breadth first (every step, one or two details each), then depth on request: CDN, load balancer, app server, cache, database.
keyPoints: Covers all steps in order: URL parsing/HSTS, DNS, TCP, TLS (cert validation), HTTP request with cookies, response, rendering (DOM, CSSOM, JS, layout, paint) and sub-resource requests
Includes rough timings tied to RTT and notes that round trips dominate for distant users
Server side: CDN/WAF edge, load balancer terminating TLS and choosing a healthy instance
App server checks session and caches (e.g. Redis), queries the database on a miss, may call other services (ideally in parallel), renders and compresses the response
Mentions response headers (status, Content-Type, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie) and that static assets come from CDN caches
Answer is structured (outline first, offers to go deeper) rather than an unordered dump
